title: Day Bar Clocks
description: Slide a time along one day bar and read it on the 12-hour clock and the 24-hour clock, add 12 to a p.m. hour except in the 12 o'clock hour, and see why that hour is a case of its own.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Read a 24-hour time as the hours and minutes after midnight, change 12-hour times into 24-hour times by adding 12 from one o'clock on in the afternoon, treat the 12 o'clock hour on its own, and change 24-hour times back into 12-hour times.
writeup.look: One day bar from 12 midnight to 12 midnight with the 24-hour times above and the 12-hour times below, a sliding marker and a violet tile of 12 h.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Day Bar Clocks' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of times converted. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The day bar runs across the area along y 420 from x 90 to x 1130, 90 tall, with 12 midnight at the left end and 12 midnight at the right end and 12 noon marked where the halves meet. The 24-hour times stand above it along y 350 and the 12-hour times below it along y 540, all in near-black ink. The half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m., and the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m. The marker slides along the bar, amber while it is being placed. The time the question gives is set in deep blue, labelled Given, on whichever clock it is given on, and the same time is read on the other clock in green, labelled Answer, at x 120, y 650. A 24-hour time is four digits and the word hours, and a zero that holds the front place open is grey, labelled Place holder. The violet tile of 12 h, labelled Jump, waits at x 900, y 230 and is dragged onto the hour of a p.m. time from one o'clock on. On the third phase the two 12 o'clock hours are lit amber on the bar and the tile will not settle in either. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for a.m., p.m. and hours. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The last time stays on the bar with its marker, both clocks read beside it and the tile where it was used.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the tile is tried on a time in a 12 o'clock hour, it shivers and slides off, the two 12 o'clock hours on the bar glow amber once, and the time is written right without it.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet converted. On the first phase the day bar runs from 12 midnight to 12 midnight with the 24-hour times above it and the 12-hour times below, and the marker waits at the left end. On the second the marker sits on a p.m. time and the violet tile of 12 h waits beside the bar. On the third the two 12 o'clock hours stand out on the bar, one just after midnight and one just after noon, with the tile beside them. On the fourth the marker sits on a 24-hour time in deep blue and the 12-hour row waits empty. One thing moves, once: the marker or the tile gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any time set on the day bar and read on either clock, with the tile tried in any hour. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on four digits after midnight, adding 12, the 12 o'clock hour and writing a 24-hour time back on the 12-hour clock.
voiceLines: A day bar, from one midnight to the next.
How many hours after midnight? Then how many minutes?
Is it after one o'clock in the afternoon? Then what do you add to the hour?
The hour that begins at twelve is special. What would adding twelve do here?
Is it before noon or after? What do you do to the hours?
A new time on the bar. Read it on the other clock.
Free play. Slide the marker anywhere and read it on both clocks.
Look at the bar again. Which half of the day is the marker in?
You read one time on both clocks and kept the twelve o'clock hour apart.

observations.why: a time on either clock is the hours and minutes after midnight.
observations.soWhat: read a 24-hour time as the hours and minutes after midnight, in four digits and the word hours.
observations.observe: The marker was the same distance from the left end of the bar whichever clock the time was read on.

observations.why: an afternoon hour from one o'clock on has 12 h more before it than the same hour in the morning.
observations.soWhat: add 12 to a p.m. hour from one o'clock on, except in the 12 o'clock hour, and keep the minutes.
observations.observe: The tile of 12 h fitted onto the hour of an afternoon time and made it the hour of a 24-hour time.

observations.why: 12:40 a.m. is 40 min after midnight, and 12:40 p.m. is 12 h 40 min after midnight.
observations.soWhat: the hour that begins at 12 is a case of its own on both clocks, so the tile is kept off it.
observations.observe: The tile would not settle in either 12 o'clock hour.

observations.why: from 1300 hours on the hours are 13 or more, so 12 has been added, and before 1200 hours it is still the morning.
observations.soWhat: take away 12 from the hours from 1300 hours on, except in the 12 o'clock hour, and write a.m. or p.m. after the time.
observations.observe: Going back, the tile came off only from 1300 hours on, and a time before 1200 hours was called a.m.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, no colour means good or bad. The miss empties the answer slot at once (every digit, every box, a picked choice), so it is empty through the traceback; the pad re-opens empty after it.
tracebacks: Phase 1: The hour digits light up over the hours from midnight on the bar, then the time after midnight is written in full (a grey zero holds the front place of an early hour).
Phase 2: The hour of the given time lights amber, the 12 h tile sits on it, and the 24-hour time is written: the new hour, then the same minutes.
Phase 3: The 12 o'clock hour of the given time lights amber on the bar, the tile stays off beside it, and the four digits are written with the hours after midnight.
Phase 4: The half of the bar the marker sits in lights amber with its tag, the tile comes off the hours from 1300 hours on, and the 12-hour time is written with a.m. or p.m.

voice.opening: A day bar, from one midnight to the next.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Slide the marker anywhere and read it on both clocks.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again

voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3, 4: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }
